editions.title: Nvidia's Huang back, but AI rout and tariff plan keep markets on edge
editions.notification: Nvidia's governance now faces a credit warning as the US prepares tariffs on 14 trading partners.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's boardroom drama remains the story markets are watching, but it has moved on from the reinstatement itself. Jensen Huang was reinstated as chief executive on 23 November and the shares surged about 31% that day, adding nearly $1tn in value. The euphoria did not last: Nvidia fell again on Tuesday and was down a further 3.4% on Wednesday, and it remains about 37% below its October peak. Since then S&P Global has put Nvidia's AA rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing board independence, and four congressional committees and several federal bodies are still probing the affair.

The wider backdrop is a sharp AI-led sell-off that pushed US indexes into correction after Anthropic's record IPO, and spread through Asia. Asian markets bounced on Thursday as investors took the reported US tariff plan on 14 trading partners better than feared. The measures, stemming from a Section 301 investigation, are reportedly unlikely to take effect before February or March, and would add to strains with China ahead of a 10 January expiry of an interim trade deal. Oil is also firm, with Brent near $95 after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and reported mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz, while gold fell below $3,500 earlier in the week before steadying.

Elsewhere, Shenzhou-24 carried the first foreign astronaut to Tiangong, and the Chinese anti-graft campaign reached Shanghai party chief Chen Jining. Britain's reservists have been told to be ready for a possible call-up, and the UK and EU published treaties from their post-Brexit reset. Markets are also digesting a US export blacklist of Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other firms, which is rippling into Malaysia's data-centre sector.

editions.notification: Markets in correction after an AI-led rout, even as Anthropic's record IPO trades. Here is what is driving it.
editions.intro:
The AI share sell-off dominates the day. The S&P 500 closed at 6,918.45 on Friday, down 3.59% and in correction, its seventh straight losing session and longest such run since February 2020. The Nasdaq has erased its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the fall, with Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%. Anthropic's $81bn IPO, the largest ever, has been caught in the rout: it opened at $111.50, closed its debut at $97.17 and fell about 9% on Friday. Asian markets were hit hard, with Taiwan's index recording its steepest weekly drop in decades. Regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have responded with emergency steps, including Taiwan's wider short-selling ban, but South Korea's KOSPI still fell 5% on Monday despite pledges of stabilisation funds.

Behind the sell-off are worries about debt-funded AI spending. Reports that Nvidia's $100bn OpenAI deal may not proceed, and reports that Anthropic has around $900bn of spending commitments that could be rated junk, have revived fears of a bubble. Nvidia's leadership is also in turmoil. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive over an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive US intelligence has reportedly linked to Chinese espionage. Bessent now says he would not oppose a return, though Colette Kress remains interim chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under growing pressure over chip sales to China.

Away from markets, Andy Burnham's UK-EU reset deals on trade, emissions and youth mobility are drawing fire, with student fees still unresolved. Democrats won their largest House majority since the early 1990s. A Lean verification of an Anthropic claim on the Riemann hypothesis adds a notable tech story, though it still needs human review.

editions.notification: Anthropic's record IPO couldn't stop an AI rout: S&P 500 in correction and Asian markets heading for their worst week since 2020.
editions.intro:
Markets are the main story. Anthropic's $81bn Nasdaq debut at $83 a share was the largest IPO on record, but the shares have since slid and the wider AI trade has sold off hard. The S&P 500 fell 3.59% on Friday to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and more than 10% below its October record, which puts it in correction. The Dow has also entered correction, the Nasdaq has given up its 2026 gains, and Taiwan, Japan and South Korea have fallen sharply. Nvidia, still without a permanent chief after Jensen Huang's resignation and an affair scandal, has been among the heaviest fallers, and the SEC and California's attorney general are now probing the company.

The Gulf and Ukraine are the other pressure points. Iran fired missiles and drones at US sites in Kuwait and Bahrain after US strikes near Hormuz, the second military exchange since a memorandum of understanding was signed last week. Trump is reportedly weighing new strikes on Iran, and oil markets are watching closely. On the diplomatic side, Trump, Xi and Putin met at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, but produced only a broad four-point declaration and no breakthroughs on nuclear arms. Europeans fret about being sidelined. Meanwhile a Russian cruise missile crashed in Poland during a NATO exercise, and Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge again.

At home, Andy Burnham signed a reset deal with the EU covering food, carbon trading and a youth mobility scheme for up to 100,000 people a year. Farage and Badenoch attacked it, and the EU has tied parts of it to tuition fees for EU students. Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, and the Bank of England has raised rates to 4%.

Fashion.title: Burberry rebounds as Capri names new CEO
Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Tech.title: Huawei convicted in US fraud and trade-secret trial
Tech.notification: A Brooklyn jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including fraud and trade-secret theft. Sentencing is set for September 2027.
Tech.summary:
A Brooklyn federal jury has convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. The company was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and of conspiring to obstruct justice. Prosecutors said Huawei lied to banks about business in Iran and North Korea. Judge Ann Donnelly will sentence the company in September 2027, and penalties could run into billions of dollars.

The verdict lands alongside a widening scandal in the chip sector. Scrutiny of Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, has grown after reports linking her to Chinese intelligence and to chip smuggling. Senator John Kennedy wants Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to testify under oath. Nvidia says it has stopped H200 shipments to China, and its shares fell sharply in the latest session.

Elsewhere, AI concerns continue to shape the sector. Anthropic shares slipped below their IPO price, Amazon agreed a deal reportedly worth around $7.5bn for Decart's chip-optimisation technology, and Meta launched its Muse agent in the UK.

Finance.title: Nvidia governance under scrutiny as AI stocks wobble
Finance.notification: S&P puts Nvidia's AA rating on downgrade watch as board independence is questioned
Finance.summary:
Nvidia's governance has become the market's main worry. S&P Global has placed the chipmaker's AA rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing board tenures that may have weakened directors' independence. The shares are about 38% below their 6 October level, and four congressional committees and several probes are still open, with Jensen Huang due to testify next week.

The wider AI trade is wobbling too. The Nasdaq fell sharply on Tuesday and US indices closed lower on Wednesday, while Asian markets suffered their steepest slide since 2020 before a partial rebound. Concerns about the payoff from AI spending, US midterm results that may bring tougher AI rules, and a Fed that markets now see tightening in December are all weighing on sentiment.

Trade and rates add to the pressure. Washington has added Singapore and Malaysian firms to its Entity List over chip diversion, and new tariff proposals on 14 trading partners are not expected to take effect before early 2027. Bank of Japan policy is also firming, with a December hike expected.

World.title: Middle East flare-up lifts oil as Gulf attacks escalate
World.notification: Oil climbs as Houthi strikes reach Saudi Arabia and ships hit mines near Hormuz.
World.summary:
Oil prices rose again as Gulf tensions widened. Yemen's Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest, and reports said at least two ships struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent traded near $95 a barrel after a 3.5% gain on Wednesday, and the Houthis have also threatened Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports. Analysts say the attacks add to the geopolitical risk premium and threaten the recent recovery in Gulf oil flows.

For the US, the bigger market story is the trade and rate backdrop. A Section 301 tariff plan reportedly covering 14 trading partners, including China, the EU and Japan, could strain relations ahead of a China interim deal expiring on 10 January. Upbeat growth and inflation data have also pushed up bets on Federal Reserve rate rises, which weighed on gold, which fell below $3,500 an ounce before steadying near $3,580.

Elsewhere, the Army's planned detonation of lead azide in Iowa and the COP31 climate talks collapsing over fossil fuel language dominate headlines. In the UK, the MoD has asked about 100,000 reservists to be ready for a possible call-up, the first such move since the Cold War.

Fashion.title: Shein settles US claims as Europe sales slump
Fashion.notification: Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle US deceptive marketing claims, as its European sales fall 27.6%.
Fashion.summary:
Shein dominates the fashion news this cycle, and on two fronts. It has agreed to pay $100 million to settle US Federal Trade Commission claims that it misled shoppers about reviews, suppliers and where cotton was grown. The same week, its quarterly figures showed European revenue down 27.6% to $2.98 billion, hit by the EU's €3 duty on low-value parcels. The company now expects Europe not to recover until the second half of 2027, and a further €2 fee from November adds uncertainty to the year-end season.

The wider luxury and mainstream fashion picture is one of tougher trade and cost pressures. New US Section 301 tariffs on 16 trading partners could hit footwear and apparel, with hearings set for January. Bangladesh's wage row has pushed garment workers into the streets, and the minimum wage has been lifted only 36% to 17,000 taka, the smallest rise in four decades, while buyers shift orders elsewhere.

Luxury houses are sounding more confident. Bernard Arnault can now lead the Agache holding until he is 95, a change tied to the planned Agache-Dior merger that shareholders vote on in December. Retail results also pointed up: Abercrombie & Fitch, Dick's and Kohl's all raised outlooks, although Gap cut its own.
